title: From 'I saw it' to 'we know it': how a discovery wins belief

summary.text: In the 1670s, a Dutch cloth seller wrote to the great scientists of London that a single drop of water was full of tiny living beings. Nobody believed him. Nobody else had a lens strong enough to look. How does a claim that nobody can check become something everybody knows? Your child makes a lens from one drop of water, finds out what it shows in a newspaper photograph, and then hands the steps to someone else to see if they get the same result. They also set up the three jars of a famous fly test, and meet people whose ideas were doubted for years before they were believed.
summary.art: A girl holding a strip of foil with a drop of water in a tiny hole over a newspaper photograph, with her grandmother looking over her shoulder.

intro.hook: You tell your class that one drop of water holds living beings too small to see. You are the only person with a lens strong enough to look. Would your class believe you? Should they?
intro.text: In the 1670s this really happened to Antoni van Leeuwenhoek, a Dutch cloth seller. He made tiny lenses, looked at water and saw tiny living beings. The Royal Society in London, the most famous group of scientists of the time, did not believe what he wrote. A discovery is not finished when one person sees something. In this unit you make your own water-drop lens, find out if a stranger can follow your steps and see what you saw, and meet people whose ideas took years to be believed.
intro.art: A cloth seller in a Dutch shop holding up a tiny lens on a metal plate to his eye, with bolts of cloth behind him.

outcomes: I can explain why a discovery is not finished until other people can repeat it by following the steps.
I can write steps clear enough for a stranger to repeat my test, and check them by watching the stranger try.
I can explain how a drop of water bends light like a lens and makes small things look bigger.
I can explain why scientists doubted Leeuwenhoek and Wegener, and what finally changed their minds.
I can tell how Redi tested the old idea that maggots come from rotting meat, and what each of his three jars showed.
I can give reasons why good ideas are rejected and why wrong ideas are kept, with an example of each.
I can name people whose careful work behind a discovery is often left out of the story, and say what they did.

terms.meaning: The steps you follow to find something out, written clearly enough that someone else could follow them.
terms.example: A recipe for idli batter is a method. Anyone who follows it can make idli.
terms.art: A recipe card with numbered steps beside a steel plate of idlis.

terms.meaning: To do a test again by following the same steps, to see if you get the same result. Scientists also call this replicating.
terms.example: A friend follows your written steps and gets the same answer as you.
terms.art: Two children at two tables doing the same experiment from the same page of steps.

terms.meaning: A curved piece of clear material, such as glass or water, that bends light.
terms.example: The glass in a pair of spectacles is a lens.
terms.art: A pair of spectacles on a table with a beam of light passing through one glass.

terms.meaning: The bending of light when it passes from one clear material into another, such as from air into water.
terms.example: A straw in a tumbler of water looks bent where it meets the water.
terms.art: A straw standing in a clear tumbler of water, looking broken at the water line.

terms.meaning: To make something look bigger than it really is.
terms.example: A lens magnifies small print so you can read it.
terms.art: A magnifying glass held over a line of small print, with the letters looking larger inside the glass.

terms.meaning: A tool with one or more lenses that makes tiny things big enough to see.
terms.example: A school microscope shows the cells of an onion skin.
terms.art: A school microscope on a table with a slide on its stage.

terms.meaning: Not believing a claim yet, and asking for it to be checked. Good doubt asks to see the evidence. It is not rude.
terms.example: "Can I try it myself?" is a polite way to doubt.
terms.art: A girl with her head tilted and one eyebrow raised, looking at a friend who is holding out a small foil strip.

terms.meaning: A group of scientists in London, started in 1660, who met to share and test new discoveries. Its motto means: take nobody's word for it.
terms.example: The Royal Society asked for Leeuwenhoek's claim to be checked before they believed it.
terms.art: Men in long coats around a table in a London room, looking at a small brass instrument and a stack of letters.

terms.meaning: The old idea that living things, such as maggots, can appear on their own from non-living things, such as rotting meat or mud.
terms.example: Many people once thought flies were made by rotting meat.
terms.art: A piece of meat on a plate with a cloud above it marked with a question mark and tiny flies drawn inside.

terms.meaning: A thin, loose cloth with tiny holes. It lets air and smells through but keeps out flies.
terms.example: A thin muslin cloth tied over a jar is gauze.
terms.art: A jar covered with thin cloth held by a rubber band, with a fly resting on top.

terms.meaning: How something works: the push or process that makes it happen.
terms.example: A pulley is the mechanism that lifts a bucket from a well.
terms.art: A well with a wooden pulley and a rope lifting a bucket.

terms.meaning: The remains or print of a plant or animal from long ago, kept in rock.
terms.example: A fossil fern leaf can be found in coal.
terms.art: A piece of dark rock with the pressed print of a fern leaf on its face.

terms.meaning: The idea, put forward by Alfred Wegener in 1912, that the continents very slowly move across the Earth.
terms.example: Wegener said South America and Africa were once joined and have moved apart.
terms.art: A map with South America and Africa drawn side by side, fitting together like puzzle pieces.

terms.meaning: The modern idea that Earth's outer shell is broken into big pieces, called plates, that move slowly and carry the continents with them.
terms.example: India sits on a plate that is pushing into Asia, and this helps lift the Himalayas.
terms.art: A cross-section of Earth showing plates as large slabs pushing into one another at the Himalayas.

terms.meaning: A tool for observing or measuring, such as a thermometer, a rain gauge or a lens.
terms.example: A rain gauge is an instrument that measures how much rain has fallen.
terms.art: A rain gauge standing in an open field with a measuring tube beside it.

terms.meaning: A word that Leeuwenhoek used for the tiny living things he saw in water. It means little animals. Today we call many of them bacteria or single-celled beings.
terms.example: The animalcules in pond water swim, turn and feed, though each is too small to see without a lens.
terms.art: A drawing of tiny round and oval creatures swimming in a circle that shows a water drop under a lens.

explanations.concept: A discovery is finished when others can repeat it
explanations.definition: A discovery is not complete when one person sees something. It is complete when other people, following the same steps, can see it too.
explanations.description: Suppose you see something nobody else has seen. Maybe you are right. But how would anyone know? You might have made a mistake, or been fooled by your own eyes, or been the only one with the right tool. So scientists ask for the steps. If other people follow your steps and get the same result, the result stops being only yours and becomes shared knowledge. This is called repeating a test. In 1989 two chemists announced a way to make energy in a jar of water at room temperature. Labs around the world followed their steps and could not get the same result, and the claim was dropped.
examples: Anjana sees dots in a newspaper photograph. Her cousin follows her steps and sees them too.
A friend gets a different answer from yours when following your steps. This tells you a step is unclear.
A result that nobody else can repeat is set aside until someone can.
explanations.art: Two people at separate tables, each holding a foil lens over a newspaper photo, looking at the same page of steps.
explanations.context: This card explains why a discovery is only finished when others can repeat it.

explanations.concept: A method: steps that a stranger can follow
explanations.definition: A method is a list of steps written so well that a stranger, without you in the room, can follow them and get the same kind of result.
explanations.description: Writing steps sounds easy, but most first tries are not clear enough. 'Make a hole' leaves out the size of the hole, the tool, and which side is up. 'Hold it close' leaves out how close. A clear step names the amount, the tool, the place and the time. For example: 'Press the tip of a sharp pencil once into the foil, on a folded towel, then twist.' A good method also says what you should see, so a reader knows if they are on track, and what often goes wrong. The best test of your steps is to watch a stranger follow them while you say nothing.
examples: 'Add some water' is unclear. 'Add one drop of water from a toothpick tip' is clear.
'Look closely' is unclear. 'Put your eye as close as one finger-width from the foil' is clear.
A recipe that gives the amount of salt, not just 'some', works for any cook.
explanations.art: A notebook page with numbered steps, one circled in red as unclear, and a second child reading it with a puzzled face.
explanations.context: This card explains what makes the steps of a test clear enough to repeat.

explanations.concept: How a drop of water becomes a lens
explanations.definition: Light bends when it passes from air into water. A round drop of water bends the light from a small thing so that it spreads wider, and the thing looks bigger.
explanations.description: Light travels slower in water than in air, so when it crosses the surface at a slant, it bends. This is called refraction. A flat surface bends all the light the same way. A curved surface bends the light more at the edge than at the middle. A drop of water sitting in a tiny hole is held in a round shape because water particles pull on each other. The pull is called surface tension. The round drop acts as a lens. A smaller, rounder drop bends light more than a larger, flatter one, so it magnifies more. Glass lenses, spectacles, cameras and the lens in your own eye all work by bending light in a similar way.
examples: A straw in a tumbler of water looks bent, because light bends at the water's surface.
A drop of water on a newspaper makes the print under it look bigger.
A glass of water with a flat side acts like a weak lens, and a round glass bowl acts like a stronger one.
explanations.art: A cross-section of a round water drop in a foil hole, with lines of light bending as they enter and spread out towards an eye.
explanations.context: This card explains why a drop of water can magnify, and why a smaller drop magnifies more.

explanations.definition: An instrument is a tool that lets us see or measure what our senses cannot. Each new tool shows us a part of the world that we did not know was there.
explanations.description: Our eyes cannot see things that are too small, too far away or too faint. In 1665 an English scientist, Robert Hooke, published drawings of a flea, a louse and the cells of cork, seen through a microscope with several lenses. He gave cells their name. Leeuwenhoek used a different design with just one very small and very good lens, strong enough to show living beings in water. Telescopes opened the sky in the same way. A new tool does not just add facts. It can show that something we thought was empty, like a drop of water, is full of life. Every tool also has limits. It shows only what it was built to show, and it can make things look a little different from how they really are, so people must learn how to read what it shows.
examples: A microscope shows bacteria and single-celled beings in a drop of pond water.
A telescope shows moons around Jupiter.
A thermometer shows a temperature that your fingers cannot judge exactly.
explanations.art: A microscope, a telescope and a thermometer in a row, each with a small picture above it of what it shows.
explanations.context: This card explains how new tools make new discoveries possible.

explanations.concept: Why scientists doubted Leeuwenhoek, and why doubt is part of the work
explanations.definition: Doubt means asking for a claim to be checked before believing it. It is a normal part of science, and the motto of the Royal Society says it: take nobody's word for it.
explanations.description: Leeuwenhoek had no university degree. He wrote in Dutch, and he kept the way he made his lenses secret. In the 1670s he told the Royal Society in London that a drop of water held thousands of tiny moving beings. The members had never seen such a thing, and their own microscopes were not strong enough. So they doubted him. Doubting him was not rude. It was what the Royal Society's motto asked for. After some effort, Robert Hooke and others in London made strong lenses of their own, followed Leeuwenhoek's description, and saw the same creatures in 1677. Leeuwenhoek was then respected, and in 1680 he was made a member of the Society. Doubt, followed by checking, turned his claim into knowledge.
examples: A friend says she saw a shooting star. You ask where and when, and look yourself.
A claim that no one can check gets set aside until someone can.
A polite doubter says: 'Can I try it myself?' and does not say 'You are wrong.'
explanations.art: Men in a London room gathered around a table, one holding a letter and another looking through a brass microscope.
explanations.context: This card explains why the Royal Society doubted Leeuwenhoek and how doubt led to checking.

explanations.concept: An old idea that was wrong: life from rotting meat
explanations.definition: Spontaneous generation was the idea that some living things appear from non-living things. Francesco Redi tested it for flies in 1668 and showed it was wrong.
explanations.description: For thousands of years, many people believed that maggots were made by rotting meat. They saw maggots on meat again and again, so the idea seemed sensible. Redi, an Italian doctor, wondered if flies were laying eggs that people did not see. He put pieces of meat in several jars. Some jars stayed open. Some were sealed. Some were covered with a thin cloth that let the smell through but not the flies. Maggots appeared in the open jars. They did not appear on the meat in the sealed jars. On the cloth, flies laid eggs, but the maggots could not reach the meat. Redi's test was easy to repeat, and others did. A different version of the question was about microbes, which are living things too small to see. It was not settled until the 1860s, when Louis Pasteur showed that microbes in broth come from microbes in the air.
examples: Maggots on open meat come from fly eggs, not from the meat.
Mould on bread grows from tiny spores in the air, not from the bread itself.
A closed jar of boiled broth stays clear until a microbe gets in.
explanations.art: Three jars of meat: an open one with flies, a sealed one with none, and a cloth-covered one with flies on the cloth.
explanations.context: This card explains how Redi tested the old idea that flies come from rotting meat.

explanations.concept: Why good ideas are sometimes rejected: drifting continents
explanations.definition: A good idea can be rejected for years if it has no explanation for how it could work, and if it goes against what most experts believe.
explanations.description: In 1912, Alfred Wegener, a German weather scientist, said the continents were once joined and have drifted apart. He had evidence. South America and Africa fit like puzzle pieces. The same kinds of fossils, such as the fern Glossopteris and a freshwater reptile called Mesosaurus, are found on coasts now thousands of kilometres apart. Rock layers match across the ocean. But he could not name a force strong enough to move continents, and he was not a geologist. Most geologists rejected the idea. Wegener died in 1930 on an expedition in Greenland. In the 1960s, maps of the ocean floor and the magnetism in rocks showed that the sea floor spreads, and the continents ride on moving plates. Wegener's idea was accepted, in a new form. Geologists named the old southern continent Gondwana, after a region of central India.
examples: India was once part of Gondwana, and it moves north by about 5 centimetres a year.
Glossopteris fossils are found in India, Africa, South America, Australia and Antarctica.
An idea with strong evidence but no mechanism can wait decades to be believed.
explanations.art: Today's map of the world with arrows showing the continents once joined into one landmass, with India next to Antarctica and Africa.
explanations.context: This card explains why Wegener's idea of drifting continents was rejected for decades, and what changed.

explanations.concept: The woman who mapped the sea floor: Marie Tharp
explanations.definition: Many discoveries rest on people who collect measurements and draw them, not only on the person whose name is on the idea. Marie Tharp is one example.
explanations.description: In the 1950s, Marie Tharp worked at a research centre in New York. For years, women were not allowed on research ships, so she could not collect depth readings herself. She drew the maps from the numbers that others brought back. Along the middle of the Atlantic Ocean, she noticed a deep valley in the ridge. Her colleague Bruce Heezen at first thought she must be wrong, because a valley like that would fit the idea of moving continents, which he did not believe. Then he found that earthquakes lined up along the same valley. Together they made maps of the ocean floor that helped to convince scientists that the sea floor is spreading. Her story shows how a pattern can be seen by the person who looks at all the numbers, and how it can take time for even a colleague to believe it.
examples: A person who draws a map from thousands of depth numbers sees a pattern that no single number shows.
A colleague can doubt you and then change their mind when new evidence arrives.
Credit often goes to the person who explains the pattern, and less to the person who drew it.
explanations.art: A woman at a drawing board in a laboratory, drawing the profile of an ocean ridge from long strips of depth numbers.
explanations.context: This card tells how Marie Tharp saw a pattern in the sea floor and what happened when she shared it.

explanations.description: Wrong ideas stay for reasons. They can seem sensible, as with maggots on meat. They may be taught by respected people, so doubting them feels rude. A good story can feel more satisfying than a plain fact. And sometimes nobody has done the simple test. Thinkers still argue about how much of this is human nature and how much is how groups of people work. We may not be able to stop wrong ideas from seeming sensible, from being taught by respected people or from making a good story. But we can build habits against them, such as asking 'who tested this?' and trying the test ourselves.
examples: A teacher repeats a saying that nobody has ever tested.
A nice story about a famous scientist spreads, though parts of it were added later.
A simple test, like Redi's jars, is not tried for many years.
explanations.art: A crowd all nodding at a speaker on a platform, while a small girl at the back holds up a hand with a question.
explanations.context: This card gives some reasons why wrong ideas stay for a long time, and says honestly that thinkers still discuss them.

explanations.definition: Behind many discoveries stand the people who observe carefully, draw, build instruments and keep records. They are often left out of the story.
explanations.description: Maria Sibylla Merian, a German artist and naturalist born in 1647, began raising silkworms as a girl. At that time many people believed insects came from mud. She raised caterpillars at home, watched each change, and drew the whole life of each insect, from egg to caterpillar to chrysalis to moth or butterfly, with the plant the insect ate. Her books of paintings appeared in 1679 and later, and in 1705 she published a famous book on the insects of Suriname. Anna Mani, born in 1918 in Peermade in Kerala, studied physics, and worked for the India Meteorological Department in Pune. She designed and tested instruments for measuring sunshine, wind and ozone, so that weather scientists in India could measure the sky properly. C. V. Raman won the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1930 for the Raman effect. His student K. S. Krishnan worked beside him on the experiments and was not named in the prize.
examples: A picture of the life of an insect is a record that others can check.
An instrument that gives the same reading for everyone makes weather science possible.
A student who runs the experiment may not be named when the prize is given.
explanations.art: A woman in a long dress painting a caterpillar on a leaf at a table in the 1600s, with jars of caterpillars behind her.
explanations.context: This card names some people whose careful work stands behind big discoveries.

explanations.concept: Some skills cannot be fully written down
explanations.description: Even the best steps cannot say everything. Making a good water drop needs a feel in the fingers that comes from trying. Michael Polanyi, a scientist and philosopher, wrote that we know more than we can tell. People learn some skills by watching and doing, not by reading. This does not mean steps are useless. It means that sometimes the best way to repeat a test is to learn it from someone who has done it, and then to write the steps better. Scientists still argue about how much of knowledge can be written down.
examples: A cook can describe how soft the dough should feel, but a child learns it only by touching dough.
A pupil learns to ride a bicycle by trying, not by reading steps.
A tailor can feel when cloth is right before a measuring tape says it.
explanations.art: An old woman guiding a child's hands as they knead dough together on a steel plate.
explanations.context: This card says that written steps help a great deal, but some skills pass best from person to person.

explanations.concept: Lone geniuses, or times that were ready?
explanations.description: Do discoveries come from rare, brilliant people? Or do they come when the tools, the questions and the knowledge of the time are ready? Thinkers disagree. Both views have examples. Many discoveries were made by several people at nearly the same time.
examples: Charles Darwin and Alfred Russel Wallace each reached the idea of natural selection in the 1850s.
Isaac Newton and Gottfried Leibniz each invented calculus, working apart.

perspectives.explanation: A few people have unusual insight, and without them a discovery would come much later, or not at all.
When the tools, the questions and the knowledge are ready, someone will find the answer. That is why so many discoveries happen twice.
Both matter. The time makes a discovery possible, and a person's care and courage decide who finds it and how well it is shared.

explanations.art: Two scientists at desks in different countries, both writing the same idea in their notebooks, with a clock on the wall between them.
explanations.context: This card is about a question people still argue over: do discoveries come from rare geniuses, or do they come when the time is ready for them?

agreed.text: Light bends when it passes between air and water, and a curved water surface can make small things look bigger.
agreed.evidence: Anyone can make a water-drop lens and see print look bigger. Measurements show that light bends by the same rule in glass, in water and in the lens of the eye.

agreed.text: The tiny living beings that Leeuwenhoek saw in water are real.
agreed.evidence: Hooke and others saw them in 1677, and microscopes since then have shown bacteria and single-celled beings in water everywhere.

agreed.text: Flies come from eggs laid by flies, not from rotting meat.
agreed.evidence: Many people have repeated Redi's test with open, sealed and cloth-covered jars. Maggots appear only where flies could lay eggs.

agreed.text: The continents move very slowly on large plates, a few centimetres each year.
agreed.evidence: Satellite measurements can now show the movement directly. Maps of the sea floor, matching rocks and fossils on separate coasts, and magnetism in sea-floor rocks all agree.

agreed.text: A result that only one person can get is weaker than one that many people can get from the same written steps.
agreed.evidence: In 1989 two chemists announced a way to make energy in a jar of water at room temperature, which was called cold fusion. Labs that followed their steps did not find it.

agreed.text: Doubting a new claim is part of how science works, and good doubt asks for a check and does not insult.
agreed.evidence: The Royal Society, started in 1660, chose the motto 'take nobody's word for it'. Leeuwenhoek's claim became accepted because others checked.

challenging.claim: Discoveries are made by lone geniuses.
challenging.who: A popular idea, found in many old books
challenging.for: Some people have unusual insight, and some discoveries were made by one person working alone for years.
challenging.against: Leeuwenhoek's claim needed Hooke and others to repeat it. Wegener's idea needed sea-floor maps drawn by Tharp and others. Many discoveries were made twice at the same time. Discoveries are built by many hands.
challenging.context: This card is about the idea that one lone genius makes every discovery.

challenging.claim: If most experts reject an idea, it must be wrong.
challenging.for: Most ideas that experts reject are wrong, and experts are right far more often than not.
challenging.against: Wegener's idea of drifting continents was rejected by most geologists for about fifty years, and it was right. What decides is the evidence, not how many people agree.
challenging.context: This card is about the idea that an idea rejected by most experts is always wrong.

challenging.claim: A discovery counts as soon as someone first sees it.
challenging.for: Someone had to be the first, and their seeing was real.
challenging.against: If nobody else can repeat what the person saw, nobody can tell a discovery from a mistake. Leeuwenhoek was believed only after Hooke looked for himself in 1677 and saw the same thing.
challenging.context: This card is about whether a discovery counts as soon as the first person sees it.

challenging.claim: People who held wrong ideas in the past were foolish.
challenging.for: We know more now than people did then.
challenging.against: The idea that maggots come from meat was sensible, because people saw maggots on meat again and again. It took a clever test to tell apart the two ideas: that the meat makes the maggots, or that flies lay eggs on the meat. People in the past used the evidence they had, as we do.
challenging.context: This card is about the idea that people who believed wrong things in the past were foolish.

challenging.claim: Written steps can always carry a skill from one person to another.
challenging.who: Some scientists who like clear methods
challenging.for: Clear steps let strangers repeat many tests, which is how science spreads.
challenging.against: Some skills, like making a good water drop or kneading dough, pass best by watching and doing. Michael Polanyi argued that we know more than we can say.
challenging.context: This card is about whether written steps can carry every skill.

big_questions.q: If only you can see something and nobody can check it, is it a discovery or only a story?
big_questions.hint: Think about Leeuwenhoek's letters. When did his claim change from a story to knowledge?

big_questions.q: The tiny beings in the water were there long before anyone saw them. Did they exist before the discovery?
big_questions.hint: Think about the difference between a thing existing and a thing being known.

big_questions.q: A lens bends light. How do we know it shows what is really there and not just something the lens made?
big_questions.hint: Think about how Hooke checked Leeuwenhoek with lenses of his own.

big_questions.q: Wegener was right and still rejected for fifty years. Where is the line between healthy doubt and stubbornness?
big_questions.hint: Think about what the doubters asked for and what they could not get.

big_questions.q: Some skills cannot be fully written down. Does that mean that knowledge lives in people, and not only in books?
big_questions.hint: Think about learning to make a water drop, or to knead dough.

big_questions.q: Who gets believed first: the person with the title, or the person with the evidence? Who should be?
big_questions.hint: Think about Leeuwenhoek, who had no degree, and Tharp, who was not allowed on the ships.

big_questions.q: Two people look through the same drop and describe it differently. Who is right?
big_questions.hint: Think about what they both agree on.

big_questions.q: If you could add one new tool to the world, what unseen thing would you want to see?
big_questions.hint: Think about the very small, the very far, the very slow or the very hidden.

story.title: The Dots in the Newspaper
story.note: A made-up story. The science in it is real: pictures in newspapers are printed as tiny dots in rows, and a water drop in a small hole makes a simple lens. The dots look like yellow, pink, blue and black in colour pictures.
text: Every morning in Thrissur, Ammamma sat on the verandah with a glass of filter coffee and the newspaper. She read every page, even the tiny advertisements, with her glasses low on her nose. Anjana was ten and staying for the holidays. She sat beside her on the cool floor.

On Tuesday there was a big photograph on the front page. It showed the Pooram, with elephants standing under bright, shining umbrellas. "A real photograph," said Ammamma, tapping it. "Seeing is believing. A picture does not lie."

Anjana put her hand in her pocket. A week ago, at her school science club, she had made a lens from a strip of kitchen foil with a tiny hole in it and a drop of water in the hole. She had kept it ever since. "Ammamma, can I look at the picture with this?"
She rested the foil on two small stacks of coins above the paper and put her eye close. She moved her head up and down, a hair at a time, until the colours swam into focus. Her mouth fell open.
The elephants' umbrellas were not smooth. They were made of dots. Tiny dots in rows, yellow and pink and blue and black, far too small to see without the drop.
"Ammamma! The picture is made of dots!"
Ammamma smiled kindly, the way she smiled at children who gave a wrong answer. "Anjana. I taught school for forty years. A photograph is a photograph. You are seeing a trick of the water."
"But I saw it!"
"I am sure you saw something," said Ammamma. "That is not the same as the picture being made of dots."

Anjana held out the foil. Ammamma took off her glasses and held it the way she thought it should go. "I see a wet blur," she said. "And my own eyelash." Anjana's cousin Vishnu was called from the kitchen. He saw a bright smear, and then he dropped the foil in the coffee.

Anjana sat on the step with hot ears. She was sure about the dots. Ammamma was sure about the picture. If only she could see what Anjana saw, there would be nothing to argue about. But she could not, and Anjana did not know why.

Her aunt Remya came out with a towel. "Anju. Ammamma is not saying you are wrong. She is saying she cannot see it. You know what your teacher says. A discovery is not finished until someone else can do it."
"Miss Sheela says to write the steps so a stranger can follow them," said Anjana slowly. "Without me in the room."

She fetched her notebook and wrote, Step 1: Make a hole. She stopped. How big? With what? Which way up? She looked at the foil in the coffee. Ammamma had held it too high, like looking through a window. It had to be almost touching the paper. Anjana had never said so. She had only done it with her hands, without thinking.

She wrote seven steps. Press the tip of a sharp pencil once into the foil on a folded towel, and twist. Touch a toothpick tip, wet with one drop of water, to the hole. Rest the foil on two stacks of two coins on the picture. Put your eye as close to the foil as one finger-width. Move your head up and down very slowly until the colours sharpen. She read them twice, crossed out "close" and wrote "one finger-width" instead.
She gave Vishnu the notebook, a fresh foil strip, a toothpick and a cup of water. "I am not allowed to help," she said. "Only the words." She sat on her hands.
Vishnu read the steps with his tongue sticking out. The first drop fell through. The second stayed. For five minutes he moved his head up and down. Then he went very still. "Anju. Dots."
"What colours?" she whispered.
"Yellow. Pink. In rows. Like a kolam."

Mrs. Prameela from next door, a retired science teacher, came over for her usual chat. Remya handed her the notebook. She followed the steps one by one. "I see dots," she said, "but mine look bigger than Vishnu's, and my rows are slanted."
"Your drop is bigger," said Anjana, looking at the foil. "Mine is smaller."
"So three of us have seen three slightly different pictures of the same thing," said Mrs. Prameela, pleased. "And all of them are dots in rows. That is good evidence."

Ammamma had been watching with her arms folded. At last she said, "Give me the words, not the foil." She read the steps aloud, slowly, and did them one at a time with her glasses off. Then she was quiet for a long while.

"Forty years I have read this paper," she said, "and it was dots all along." She held the page up to the light. "I did not believe you, because I could not see it. And I could not see it because nobody had told me how."
"I only saw it first," said Anjana. "The steps showed it to everyone else."
Ammamma laughed and folded the newspaper. "Tomorrow we look at the Onam sale advertisement," she said. "Let us see what else this paper has been hiding."
story.epiphany: Anjana saw the dots first, but Ammamma could not believe it until she could see them too. What changed Ammamma's mind was not Anjana's word. It was a set of steps clear enough for others to follow. When three people followed the steps and each saw dots, the claim became something they all knew. Their pictures were not exactly alike, and that did not weaken the finding. They all agreed on dots in rows.
ask: Why could Ammamma not see the dots the first time?
What did Anjana have to add to her steps so that a stranger could follow them?
Why was it good evidence that three people saw slightly different pictures that were all dots in rows?
Why did Anjana stay out of the way and sit on her hands?
What changed Ammamma's mind in the end?

games.title: Mixed-Up Roads: put each discovery in order
games.context: This is a card game about the road a discovery travels, from the first look to being believed. Four roads are mixed together. You sort the cards into roads, and then put each road in order.

printables.title: 24 road cards: a step on the front, the step number and the reason on the back

items.f: LEEUWENHOEK'S DROP. Antoni van Leeuwenhoek, a cloth seller in Delft, makes tiny lenses to look closely at thread.
items.b: Step 1 of 6. The road starts with a tool and a curious person.

items.f: LEEUWENHOEK'S DROP. He looks at a drop of water through a lens and sees tiny things swimming.
items.b: Step 2 of 6. He has now seen something new, but only he has seen it.

items.f: LEEUWENHOEK'S DROP. He writes a letter to the Royal Society in London to tell them what he saw.
items.b: Step 3 of 6. He shares the claim, so others can judge it.

items.f: LEEUWENHOEK'S DROP. Members of the Royal Society doubt it, because nobody else has a lens as strong as his.
items.b: Step 4 of 6. Doubt is a normal step. They ask for it to be checked.

items.f: LEEUWENHOEK'S DROP. Robert Hooke and others in London follow his description and see the same tiny creatures in 1677.
items.b: Step 5 of 6. Others repeat it and the claim becomes stronger.

items.f: LEEUWENHOEK'S DROP. The Royal Society accepts his reports, and later makes him a member.
items.b: Step 6 of 6. The discovery is now shared knowledge.

items.f: REDI'S JARS. Many people say that maggots are made by rotting meat itself.
items.b: Step 1 of 6. The road starts with an old idea that most people accept.

items.f: REDI'S JARS. Francesco Redi wonders if flies are laying eggs on the meat that nobody sees.
items.b: Step 2 of 6. He asks a question that can be tested.

items.f: REDI'S JARS. In 1668 Redi puts meat in three jars: one open, one sealed, and one covered with a thin cloth.
items.b: Step 3 of 6. He designs a test with a comparison.

items.f: REDI'S JARS. Maggots appear in the open jar, and the sealed jar stays free of maggots.
items.b: Step 4 of 6. The first result points to flies, not meat.

items.f: REDI'S JARS. On the cloth, flies lay eggs, but the maggots cannot reach the meat.
items.b: Step 5 of 6. The cloth lets the smell through and keeps the flies out, so the flies must be the cause.

items.f: REDI'S JARS. Redi writes up the test so that others can do it too.
items.b: Step 6 of 6. A test others can repeat spreads the result.

items.f: WEGENER'S CONTINENTS. Alfred Wegener, a German weather scientist, sees that South America and Africa fit like puzzle pieces.
items.b: Step 1 of 6. The road starts with something noticed.

items.f: WEGENER'S CONTINENTS. He finds the same kinds of fossils on coasts that are now oceans apart.
items.b: Step 2 of 6. He looks for more evidence.

items.f: WEGENER'S CONTINENTS. In 1912 he says that the continents were once joined and have drifted apart.
items.b: Step 3 of 6. He shares the idea.

items.f: WEGENER'S CONTINENTS. Many geologists reject it, because he cannot name a force strong enough to move continents.
items.b: Step 4 of 6. An idea without a mechanism meets doubt.

items.f: WEGENER'S CONTINENTS. In 1930 Wegener dies on an expedition in Greenland, and his idea is still not accepted.
items.b: Step 5 of 6. Belief can take longer than a lifetime.

items.f: WEGENER'S CONTINENTS. In the 1960s, new maps of the sea floor and rock magnetism show that the ground does move, and his idea is accepted in a new form.
items.b: Step 6 of 6. New tools and new evidence finally changed minds.

items.f: THARP'S SEA FLOOR. Marie Tharp draws maps of the ocean floor from depth numbers that others bring back, because women are not allowed on the research ships.
items.b: Step 1 of 6. The road starts with a person who is kept off the ships but looks at all the numbers.

items.f: THARP'S SEA FLOOR. She notices a deep valley running along the middle of a ridge in the Atlantic.
items.b: Step 2 of 6. A pattern appears only when all the numbers are drawn together.

items.f: THARP'S SEA FLOOR. Her colleague Bruce Heezen at first thinks she must be wrong.
items.b: Step 3 of 6. Even a colleague can doubt a surprising result.

items.f: THARP'S SEA FLOOR. Records of earthquakes show that earthquakes line up along the same valley.
items.b: Step 4 of 6. A new kind of evidence points the same way.

items.f: THARP'S SEA FLOOR. After checking again, Heezen becomes convinced that she is right.
items.b: Step 5 of 6. The doubter is persuaded by evidence.

items.f: THARP'S SEA FLOOR. Their maps of the sea floor help persuade scientists that the sea floor is spreading.
items.b: Step 6 of 6. The map carries the discovery to everyone else.

Sort the cards into four roads by the name at the start of each card. Put each heading above its road.
Put the six cards of each road in the order they happened. The first card is where the road begins. The last is where the discovery is believed.
Turn the cards over to check. The back says the step number. One point for every card in the right place.
With friends: each player takes one road and races to put it in order. Check each other's roads. Then swap roads.
Playing alone: do the roads one at a time. Keep your score out of 24 and try to beat it next time.
When all four roads are done, find one step that all four roads have in common.

flow.do: Cut out the cards and the four road headings. Shuffle the cards. Spread them out face up. Sort them into four roads using the name at the start of each card.

flow.say: Here are six steps of Leeuwenhoek's road. Which came first? Which came last? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Put the six Leeuwenhoek cards in order. Then turn them over and check.

check.q: In Leeuwenhoek's road, the Royal Society doubted his claim. What was the main reason?
options: Nobody else had a lens strong enough to check it
They did not like Dutch people
They had never heard of water
check.why: The claim could not be checked until others had strong lenses of their own. Doubt asked for a check. A wrong pick usually means doubt was taken as rudeness and not as a request for evidence.

flow.context: In this step, you put the first road in order together.

flow.do: Do the other three roads. Your child puts each in order, then you check the backs together. Give one point for each card in the right place.
flow.say: Now do the next road. Put the six cards in order. Then we turn them over and see.
flow.kid: Put each road in order. Turn the cards over to check.

ask.q: Which road took the longest to be believed? What made it slow?
good: Wegener's. He could not say what force moved the continents.
Wegener's. It took until the 1960s and new maps of the sea floor.

flow.parent: On the Redi road, steps 4 and 5 are easy to mix up. Step 4 is about the open jar and the sealed jar. Step 5 is about the cloth-covered jar. Accept either order if your child can explain it. The back of each card gives the reason for its step.
flow.context: In this step, you put the other three roads in order and score the cards.

flow.do: Ask your child what all four roads had in common. Look for a step where someone doubted and a step where others checked.
flow.say: What step is on every road? Look for a step where someone doubted, and a step where others checked.
flow.kid: Which step is on all four roads? Look for a step where someone doubted, and a step where others checked.

ask.q: What did all four roads have in common?
good: Somebody noticed something first.
Somebody doubted.
Others checked or found more evidence before it was believed.

games.title: The Doubter and the Discoverer: a game of kind doubt
games.context: This is a two-role game. The Discoverer has a claim and must explain how to check it. The Doubter asks kind, sharp questions. Then you try the check together. You practise both parts of a discovery: showing, and doubting.

printables.title: 16 claim cards: a claim on the front and a simple check on the back

items.f: Ants follow a smell trail. If you wipe the trail, the line breaks.
items.b: Check: watch ants walking in a line. Wipe a small patch of their path with a damp cloth. The ants slow down, wander and then find the line again.

items.f: Black ink is made of many colours.
items.b: Check: put a dot of washable black felt-tip ink near the end of a strip of tissue. Dip the end in a little water. Many black inks spread out into bands of colour.

items.f: A shadow is shortest around midday.
items.b: Check: stand a pencil in clay on a sunny sill. Mark the tip of the shadow every hour. The shortest shadow is around midday. In some towns it comes up to an hour before or after 12 o'clock.

items.f: Salt makes ice melt faster.
items.b: Check: put two equal ice cubes on two plates. Sprinkle a pinch of salt on one. The salted cube melts sooner.

items.f: Sound travels through a table.
items.b: Check: put your ear on a wooden table while a friend taps the far end lightly. Then lift your head and listen to the same tap. It sounds louder through the table.

items.f: Newspaper pictures are made of tiny dots.
items.b: Check: look at a picture through a water-drop lens or a magnifying glass. You see rows of dots.

items.f: A paper towel pulls water up.
items.b: Check: stand the end of a strip of paper towel in a glass of coloured water. The colour climbs up the strip.

items.f: The Moon can be seen in the daytime.
items.b: Check: look up a Moon calendar and choose a day near the half Moon. Look at the afternoon sky. You may see the pale Moon.

items.f: Moong seeds sprout in the dark as well as in the light.
items.b: Check: wrap soaked moong in two damp cloths. Put one on a shelf and one in a dark cupboard. After two days, both have sprouts.

items.f: A raw egg floats in very salty water but sinks in plain water.
items.b: Check: a grown-up lowers an egg into a tumbler of plain water, where it sinks. Then stir in many spoons of salt until the salt disappears. The egg floats.

items.f: Warm water dissolves sugar faster than cold water.
items.b: Check: put one spoon of sugar into a glass of warm water and one into a glass of cold water. Stir the same way. Count the stirs it takes in each. The warm one takes fewer.

items.f: Blowing between two sheets of paper pulls them together.
items.b: Check: hold two sheets a few centimetres apart and blow hard between them. The sheets move towards each other.

items.f: Your two eyes see slightly different pictures.
items.b: Check: hold a finger in front of your nose and look at the far wall. Close one eye, then the other. The finger seems to jump from side to side.

items.f: A thick book and a thin book dropped together land together.
items.b: Check: hold both flat at the same height above a soft rug and let go together. They land at the same moment. Keep your feet out of the way.

items.f: A magnet can move an iron nail through paper.
items.b: Check: lay a nail on a table and cover it with a sheet of paper. Move a magnet over the paper. The nail follows the magnet.

items.f: Floating ice does not raise the water level when it melts.
items.b: Check: float ice in a glass of water and mark the level. Wait until the ice has melted. The level stays about the same.

printables.title: 8 Doubter cards: a kind, sharp question on each
items: What exactly did you do, step by step?
What did you see, and what do you think it means?
What would you see if the claim were wrong?
Did you get the same result every time?
What if I do it a different way?
What were you hoping to find?

rules: One player is the Discoverer, and the other is the Doubter. Shuffle the 16 claim cards and the 8 Doubter cards into two piles.
The Discoverer takes a claim card and reads the claim aloud. The Discoverer does not turn the card over.
The Doubter takes a Doubter card and asks the question on it, kindly. The Discoverer answers in their own words.
The Discoverer then says the steps to check the claim, so clearly that the Doubter could do them alone. The Doubter may ask one more question.
Do the check together if you have the things. Then read the back. One point to the Discoverer if the steps worked, and one to the Doubter for a good question.
Swap roles after every card. Play as many cards as you like. The most points wins, and equal scores share the win.
Playing alone: pick a claim card, write three steps to check it, do the check, then read the back and score yourself.

flow.do: Cut out the cards. Shuffle each pile. Explain that the Doubter is not rude. The Doubter asks to see the evidence.
flow.say: One of us is the Discoverer and one is the Doubter. A Doubter is not unkind. A Doubter asks to see, to try and to check.
flow.kid: One player makes a claim. The other asks kind questions.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Doubter and the Discoverer game. You set up the cards and the two roles.

flow.do: Play a practice round with the ants card. The Discoverer reads it and gives the steps. The Doubter asks one question. Do the check if you can.
flow.say: Ants follow a smell trail. If you wipe the trail, the line breaks. Doubter, what is your question? Discoverer, how would we check it?
flow.kid: Ants follow a smell trail. How would you check it?

check.q: A Discoverer says that ants follow a smell trail. Which is the best question for a Doubter to ask?
options: Everyone knows that, so why bother?
What would you see if the claim were wrong, and how could we test it?
You are wrong, because ants cannot smell.
check.why: A good Doubter asks what would count as a check. A wrong pick usually means the child thinks doubting means saying no.

flow.context: In this step, you play a practice round.

flow.say: Take a claim card and a Doubter card. Discoverer, say the steps. Doubter, listen, and try to follow them exactly.
flow.kid: Take turns. Say clear steps. Try the check.

ask.q: Which steps were the hardest to say clearly?
good: The ones where I had to say how much or how close.
The ones where I could not say what to look for.

flow.parent: If a check needs a thing you do not have, say the steps aloud and then read the back of the card. It is fine to do only some of the checks. Safety: a grown-up lowers the egg and handles ice and hot or cold water.

flow.kid: Which question helped most? Which claim surprised you?

experiments.title: The Water-Drop Lens: can someone else see what you saw?
experiments.context: In this experiment, you make three water-drop lenses with holes of different sizes and count the dots in a newspaper photograph through each one. Then you write your steps and give them to a second person, who tries the same thing from your words alone.
experiments.question: Which size of hole shows the fewest dots across the circle? The fewer the dots, the more the lens magnifies. And can a second person, who has only your written steps, put the three lenses in the same order?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. Which hole will make the dots look biggest, the small one or the big one? Will a second person, using only your written steps, put the lenses in the same order as you? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: We use the same newspaper photograph, the same patch of the picture, the same kind of water drop and the same stack of coins every time. We count the dots in the same way. Only the size of the hole changes. When the second person does it, they use fresh foil and only the written steps, and we do not help them.
results_table: About how wide the hole is
Dots across the circle: my first count
Dots across the circle: my second count
Dots across the circle: second person

materials.item: 3 strips of kitchen foil, each about 4 centimetres by 10 centimetres, with the edges folded over
a folded towel to press the foil on
a pin, a sharp pencil and a ballpoint pen, to make three holes of different sizes
a cup of water and a toothpick
a colour newspaper or magazine photograph with a flat patch of colour, such as a shirt or the sky
4 coins of the same size, to make two stacks of two
a ruler marked in millimetres, to check the hole sizes (optional)
a notebook and a pencil, and a second person who has not seen the steps

experiments.safety: A grown-up pushes the pin through the foil. Fold the foil edges over, because cut foil can be sharp. Wipe up drips so nobody slips.

schedule.what: Make three lenses, count dots through each, write the steps, let a second person try, and compare.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Then write your steps as a numbered list, with each step so clear that a stranger could follow it. Last, compare your counts with the second person's, and underline the step that was least clear.

flow.do: Tell the story of Leeuwenhoek and his lens in a few words. Ask your child to guess which hole will make the dots look biggest, and to give a reason. Write both at the top of the page.
flow.say: A cloth seller in the 1670s looked at water through a tiny lens and saw living beings. Nobody else could check. We will make our own lens and count dots in a newspaper picture. Which hole will make the dots look biggest? Why?
flow.kid: You will make three water lenses. Which hole makes the dots look biggest? Why?

ask.q: Which hole do you think will make the dots look bigger, the smaller one or the bigger one? Why?
good: A smaller drop is rounder, so it bends more light.
A bigger drop shows more, so it should be stronger.
I do not know, so we will count.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Any guess with a reason is a good start. Do not explain how the drop works yet.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Water-Drop Lens test. You guess before you build.

flow.do: Lay a foil strip on the folded towel. A grown-up pushes the pin through once, to make hole A. On the next strip press the tip of a sharp pencil once and twist for hole B. On the third strip press the ballpoint pen tip and twist for hole C.
flow.say: We make three holes of three sizes. A is the pinhole. B is the pencil hole. C is the pen hole. Write the letters on the strips.
flow.kid: Make three foil strips with three holes. Write A, B and C on them.
flow.parent: The pencil and pen holes will have rough edges. Press the rough bits flat with your thumb. The holes are about 1 millimetre, 2 millimetres and 3 to 4 millimetres across. Measure each to the nearest half millimetre against a ruler if you can.
flow.context: In this step, you make the three foil lenses.

flow.do: Choose a flat patch of colour in the photograph and ring it in pencil. Make two stacks of two coins beside the patch. Lay strip A across the stacks. Touch a wet toothpick tip to the hole to leave one drop. Put your eye close to the foil and move your head slowly until the dots look sharp.
flow.say: Look through the drop. Move your head up and down very slowly. You are looking for rows of tiny dots. Count the dots in a line across the middle of the circle.
flow.kid: Rest the foil on the coins. Add one drop. Look through it. Count the dots across.

ask.q: What do you see? How many dots are across the circle?
good: Rows of tiny coloured dots.
About 3 dots across.
It is blurry, so I will move my head.

flow.parent: If the dots look blurry, add a third coin to each stack, or take one away. If the drop falls through, make a new one with a fresh toothpick and a smaller drop. If you cannot see dots at all, count the letters of the smallest print instead. Do each hole twice and write both counts.
flow.context: In this step, you look through each lens and count the dots across the circle.

flow.do: Your child writes the steps for the whole test as a numbered list. Each step must name the tool, the amount and the place. Then read each step aloud and ask: could a stranger do this?
flow.say: Now write the steps so a stranger can do them without you. Say how big, how many and where. Read each one back to yourself.
flow.kid: Write numbered steps for a stranger. Say how big, how many and where.

check.q: Which step is clearest for a stranger to follow?
options: Make a small hole in the foil.
Put the foil on a folded towel. Press the tip of a sharp pencil once into it, and twist.
Make a hole in the foil with something sharp.
check.why: The second step names the tool, what to rest the foil on, how many presses and the twist. The others leave the reader to guess. A wrong pick usually means the child wrote the step as they would do it, not as a stranger would read it.

flow.context: In this step, you write the steps so a stranger could follow them.

flow.do: Give the second person the written steps, three fresh foil strips, the toothpick, the water, the coins and the newspaper photograph. Sit on your hands and say nothing. Watch where they get stuck and note it. They count the dots in the same way and write their numbers.
flow.say: Please follow the steps exactly. I will not help. Count the dots through each hole and write the numbers in the last column.
flow.kid: Give a stranger only your steps. Do not help. Watch where they get stuck.
flow.parent: Resist helping. If you speak, you are doing the job that the written steps should do. Write down each place where the second person stops or asks a question. Those are the steps to fix.
flow.context: In this step, a second person follows your written steps while you watch.

flow.do: Compare your counts with the second person's. Did the holes come in the same order? Fix the least clear step and write the new version.
flow.say: Do the two sets of counts agree about which hole is strongest? Where were the numbers different? Which of your steps needs fixing?
flow.kid: Compare your counts. Did the holes come in the same order? Fix one step.

ask.q: Did the second person get the same order? What does that tell you about your steps?
good: Yes, the small hole showed the fewest dots for both of us, so the steps worked.
The order was the same but the numbers were a little different.
No. One step was not clear, so I rewrote it.

flow.parent: The numbers will rarely match exactly, because hands and drops differ. What matters is whether the order matches. If the second person could not make a lens at all, the steps are the problem. That is a useful finding, not a failure.
flow.context: In this last step, you compare the results and fix the weakest step.

experiments.title: Redi's Jars: do flies come from the banana?
experiments.context: In this one-week experiment, you repeat the idea of Francesco Redi's famous test of 1668 with banana in place of meat. You use three jars: one open, one covered with thin cloth, and one with a lid. You find out where the tiny flies and maggots appear.
experiments.question: Do fruit flies, and the tiny maggots that become flies, appear in a jar of banana by themselves? Or do they appear only where flies can reach?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. In which jar will flies or maggots appear? In which will they not appear? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: All three jars are the same size, hold the same amount of banana and stand side by side in the same place. Only the cover is different: open, thin cloth, or a lid. We look at them at the same time each day and write down what we see, even on days when nothing happens.

materials.item: 3 clean glass jars or tumblers of the same size
a ripe banana, mashed, about 2 tablespoons in each jar
a piece of thin cotton cloth such as muslin, folded in two, and a rubber band
a small plate or a lid that fits one jar tightly
a marker and 3 labels or paper slips
a notebook and a pencil

experiments.safety: Do not smell the jars closely and do not open them after mould appears. Keep them out of reach of small children. If anyone has asthma or allergies, a grown-up handles the jars. Wash hands after touching. At the end, a grown-up seals the jars in a bag and throws them away.

schedule.what: Mash the banana, fill the jars, cover them, label them and set them out.
Look at each jar and write what you see.
Look at each jar and write what you see.
Look at each jar and write what you see.
Look at each jar and write what you see.
Look at each jar and write what you see.
Look for the last time, compare the jars, and decide what the test shows.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. For each jar and each day, write how many flies you see on or near the jar, any tiny white wriggling things inside, and any mould. Draw the three jars on day 7.

flow.do: Mash the banana. Put the same amount in each of the three jars. Label them OPEN, CLOTH and LID. Leave the first open. Tie the cloth over the second with the rubber band, folded double. Press the lid on the third tightly. Put the three jars side by side in the kitchen, away from direct sun.
flow.say: People once thought flies were made by rotting fruit or meat. We will test it. Which jar will have flies or maggots? Which will not? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Fill three jars with banana. Leave one open. Cover one with cloth. Close one with a lid.

ask.q: Why do we use three jars and not one?
good: So we can compare them.
So we can see what changes when the cover changes.
Because one jar would not tell us what the flies need.

flow.parent: Do not tell your child what you expect. Fruit flies usually come to a kitchen within 2 to 5 days in warm weather. If the kitchen is cold or very clean, they may take longer. Keep the jars out of the sun so the lid jar does not get hot.
flow.context: This is day 1 of Redi's Jars. You fill the jars, cover them and guess.

flow.do: Each day at about the same time, your child looks at each jar without opening it. Write the number of flies on or near it, any tiny white wriggling things inside, and any mould.
flow.say: Look at each jar. How many flies are near it? Do you see any small white wriggling things inside? Write down what you see, even if the answer is none.
flow.kid: Look at each jar. Count flies. Look for wriggling things. Write it down.
flow.wait: Do this on days 2 to 6, about four minutes each day.
flow.parent: The tiny white wriggling things look like short grains of rice. They are the young of flies, and they are called maggots. The days with nothing in a jar are as important as the days with flies. If there are no flies by day 4 in the open jar, move all three jars, together, near the fruit bowl.
flow.context: In this step, you look at the jars once a day and record what you see.

flow.do: On day 7, look one last time. Compare the three jars. Ask your child what the jars show. A grown-up seals the jars in a bag and throws them away.
flow.say: Which jars had flies near them? Which had maggots inside? What does this say about where the flies come from?
flow.kid: Compare the three jars. Where did the maggots appear? What does that show?

check.q: Maggots appeared in the open jar of banana but not in the jar with the lid. What does this show?
options: Banana makes maggots by itself
The maggots came from flies that could reach the banana
The lid made the banana go bad
check.why: The banana was the same in both jars. The maggots appeared only where flies could get in. This points to flies as the source. A wrong pick usually means the child still thinks the banana made them.

ask.q: What did the cloth-covered jar show that the lid jar could not?
good: The smell could get through the cloth, but the flies could not, and no maggots came.
Flies landed on the cloth, so they were looking for the banana, not made by it.

flow.parent: Redi saw that flies laid eggs on the gauze, and few young reached the meat. If your cloth jar has a few maggots, check whether the cloth had a gap or was thin. Report what you saw. Mould can grow in the lid jar too. Mould starts from tiny spores already on the fruit, so it is a separate matter from the flies.
flow.context: In this last step, you compare the three jars and decide what they show.
