activities.title: The Doubt Round: doubting kindly, and checking
activities.context: In this activity, a grown-up makes a surprising claim in a very sure voice. Your child practises doubting it kindly by asking questions, and then checks it by folding paper. You find out what the claim gets right and what it leaves out.

materials.item: 4 sheets of ordinary notebook paper or printer paper, all the same size
1 large sheet of thin newspaper
a pencil and a notebook, to count the folds

schedule.what: Hear the claim, ask four kind doubting questions, test it with paper, and decide what it shows.

activities.record: Write the claim. Write how many times you could fold each sheet in half. Then write one sentence about what the claim gets right and what it leaves out.

flow.do: Say in a very sure voice: you cannot fold a sheet of paper in half more than seven times. Ask your child to doubt this kindly. Offer four starter questions on a card.
flow.say: You cannot fold a sheet of paper in half more than seven times. Everyone knows it. Now doubt it kindly. You may ask: can I try it? What would show that you are wrong? Did you do it yourself?
flow.kid: Doubt the claim kindly. Ask: Can I try it? What would show that you are wrong?

ask.q: What kind question could you ask before you believe this?
good: Can I try it myself?
Did you try it, or did you hear it?
What would show that you are wrong?

flow.parent: Sound very sure at first, so your child has to ask. Then say: yes, try it. A doubter who asks to try is doing what the Royal Society asked of Leeuwenhoek.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Doubt Round. You hear a sure claim and practise doubting it kindly.

flow.do: Your child folds a sheet in half, presses the crease with a thumbnail, and folds again. Count each fold out loud. Stop when the sheet cannot be folded flat. Try three notebook sheets and the big newspaper sheet.
flow.say: Fold the sheet in half. Press the crease. Fold it again. Count each fold out loud. Stop when you cannot fold it flat.
flow.kid: Fold the paper in half again and again. Count each fold. Stop when you cannot fold.
flow.wait: Each sheet takes about a minute.
flow.parent: Most notebook sheets stop at 6 or 7 folds. A big, thin newspaper sheet may reach 7 or 8. Write down the number of folds for every sheet, even if one is different from the others. A difference between sheets is itself a finding.
flow.context: In this step, you test the claim with paper.

flow.do: Ask your child what the test showed about the claim. Then tell the story of Britney Gallivan from the parent note. Ask whether the claim was right, wrong or half right.
flow.say: What did your folds show? Was the claim right, wrong or half right? What did the claim leave out?
flow.kid: What did your folds show? Was the claim right, wrong, or half right?

check.q: A claim says paper cannot be folded in half more than seven times. A school student once folded paper twelve times, using a very long, thin roll. What does this show?
options: The claim was true for ordinary sheets but not for every kind of paper
The student cheated
Paper behaves differently in America
check.why: With ordinary sheets, the layers grow too thick and the paper too short to fold. A very long, thin roll gets past that limit. A claim can be true in some conditions and wrong in others. A wrong pick usually means the child thinks a claim must be wholly true or wholly false.

flow.parent: In 2002 Britney Gallivan, a high school student in California, worked out how long a roll of paper had to be, and folded a roll more than a kilometre long in half twelve times. She turned a popular saying into a measurable question. Each fold doubles the thickness, so 7 folds make 128 layers.
flow.context: In this last step, you decide what the test showed and what the claim left out.

setup.art: A grown-up with a stern, sure face holding up one sheet of paper while a girl on the other side of a table raises her hand to ask a question.
setup.caption: 1. Hear a sure claim. Doubt it kindly.

setup.art: A girl pressing a crease into a folded sheet of paper with her thumbnail, with five small folded stacks beside her.
setup.caption: 2. Fold again and again. Count each fold.

activities.title: Fit the Coasts: how much does a puzzle prove?
activities.context: In this activity, you trace South America and Africa from a map, cut them out and try to fit them together, as Alfred Wegener did. Then you sort pieces of evidence into those for his idea and those against it, and decide how strong the case was.

materials.item: a world map from a school atlas or a printed world map
tracing paper or thin tissue paper
blunt-ended scissors
a pencil
5 small paper slips, to write the pieces of evidence on

activities.safety: A grown-up cuts with blunt-ended scissors. Keep fingers away from the blades.

schedule.what: Trace the coasts, fit them, sort the evidence slips, and decide how strong the case is.

activities.record: Draw your fitted coasts. Under the drawing, write the five evidence slips in two lists: for the idea, and against it. Write one sentence on what you would need to be sure.

flow.do: Lay the tracing paper over South America on the map and trace it. Then trace Africa on a second piece. Cut out both shapes with blunt scissors.
flow.say: Trace South America and Africa. Cut them out. Then try to slide the two shapes together to see if they fit.
flow.kid: Trace South America and Africa. Cut them out. Try to fit them together.

ask.q: How well do the two coasts fit? Where do they not fit?
good: The bulge of Africa fits into the curve of South America.
They fit in the middle but not at the ends.

flow.parent: A grown-up helps to cut cleanly. Scientists today get the best fit by using the edge of each continent under the sea, called the continental shelf, and not the line of the beach. Your shapes will not fit perfectly, and that is worth talking about. A fit is a clue, and a clue is not a proof.
flow.context: This is the first step of Fit the Coasts. You trace two continents and try to fit them.

flow.do: Write five evidence slips. One: the coasts fit. Two: the same freshwater reptile, Mesosaurus, is found in South America and in Africa. Three: matching rock layers on both coasts. Four: nobody could name a force to move continents. Five: satellites today measure the continents moving a few centimetres each year.
flow.say: Here are five pieces of evidence. Put each into one of two piles: for Wegener's idea, or against it. Say why for each.
flow.kid: Sort five evidence slips. Which are for the idea? Which are against it?

check.q: A freshwater reptile that cannot swim across an ocean is found as a fossil on two continents now separated by ocean. What does this support?
options: The continents were once joined
The reptile was a good swimmer in salt water
The fossils are fake
check.why: A reptile that lives in fresh water could not cross an ocean. If the two lands were once joined, the reptile could live on both. This supports the idea of moving continents. A wrong pick usually means the child ignored the clue that the reptile lived in fresh water.

flow.parent: Slips 1, 2, 3 and 5 are for the idea. Slip 4 is the main one against it in 1912. Slip 5 was not known until the twentieth century. India, which is also on this map, was part of the same old southern continent, called Gondwana.
flow.context: In this step, you sort the pieces of evidence into for and against.

flow.do: Ask your child which slip made people doubt Wegener, and what had to happen for them to change their minds. Write one sentence on what you would need to be sure.
flow.say: Which slip made people doubt Wegener? What new evidence would you need to be sure? Is the fit of your two paper shapes a proof, or only a clue?
flow.kid: Which slip made people doubt Wegener? What new evidence would help?

ask.q: What evidence did people need, in the end, to change their minds?
good: A way for the continents to move.
Maps of the sea floor and rock magnetism that showed the sea floor spreads.
Satellite measurements of the movement.

flow.context: In this last step, you decide what the case needed to become convincing.

setup.art: Tracing paper laid over an atlas map with a girl tracing the outline of South America in pencil.
setup.caption: 1. Trace South America and Africa.

setup.art: Two paper cut-outs of South America and Africa pushed together on a table, with five paper slips sorted into two piles beside them.
setup.caption: 2. Fit the shapes. Sort the evidence slips into for and against.

activities.title: A String of Years: how long does belief take?
activities.context: In this activity, you cut pieces of string, one centimetre for each year, to show how long three claims waited to be believed. You compare the lengths and find out what made some quick and some slow.

materials.item: string or wool, about 3 metres
a measuring tape or a long ruler
scissors
sticky tape and three small paper labels

schedule.what: Cut three strings to the right lengths, label them, and compare.

activities.record: Draw the three strings side by side, with a label on each saying who it is for and how many years it waited.

flow.do: Tell the first story. Leeuwenhoek told London about his tiny creatures around 1674, and Hooke and others looked for themselves and saw the same creatures in 1677. That is about 3 years. Cut a 3 centimetre piece of string and label it.
flow.say: Leeuwenhoek told London about his tiny creatures around 1674. Others looked for themselves and saw the same creatures in 1677. How many years is that? Cut a piece of string, one centimetre for each year.
flow.kid: Leeuwenhoek: 1674 to 1677. How many years? Cut that many centimetres of string.
flow.context: This is the first step of A String of Years. You cut a string for Leeuwenhoek's wait.

flow.do: Tell the second story. Wegener put forward his idea in 1912, and it was accepted in the 1960s. That is about 50 years. Cut a 50 centimetre piece and label it. Hold it next to the first.
flow.say: Wegener put forward his idea in 1912. It was accepted in the 1960s. About how many years is that? Cut the string and compare.
flow.kid: Wegener: 1912 to the 1960s. About 50 years. Cut 50 centimetres of string.
flow.parent: The exact date is a matter of opinion, because acceptance came step by step through the 1960s. About 50 years is a fair round figure, so cut 50 centimetres.
flow.context: In this step, you cut a string for Wegener's wait and compare it with the first.

flow.do: Tell the third story. Redi showed in 1668 that flies do not come from meat. The wider question, whether microbes appear on their own in broth, was settled by Pasteur in the 1860s. That is about 190 years. Cut a string about 190 centimetres long, which is nearly two metres, and stretch it across the floor.
flow.say: Redi tested flies in 1668. The same idea for microbes was settled in the 1860s. About how many years is that? Cut the string and stretch it out.
flow.kid: Redi to Pasteur: 1668 to the 1860s. About 190 years. Cut a string that long.

check.q: Leeuwenhoek's claim was accepted in about 3 years, but Wegener's idea took about 50. What is the most likely reason?
options: Leeuwenhoek's claim could be checked by anyone with a good lens, but Wegener's idea needed new tools and ocean maps
Leeuwenhoek was famous
Wegener lived in a cold country
check.why: A claim that can be repeated quickly is accepted quickly. Wegener's idea needed measurements of the deep sea floor, which did not exist yet. A wrong pick usually means the child looked for a reason about the people and not about how easy the claim was to check.

ask.q: What made some claims quick to be believed and others slow?
good: Whether other people could check it easily.
Whether there was an explanation for how it works.
Whether it went against what everyone believed.

flow.context: In this last step, you cut the longest string and compare all three.

setup.art: A girl measuring and cutting three pieces of string of very different lengths on a floor, with a ruler and labels beside them.
setup.caption: 1. Cut one centimetre of string for each year of waiting.

setup.art: Three pieces of string laid side by side on a floor, a very short one, a middle one and one stretching nearly two metres.
setup.caption: 2. Compare the three strings and ask why some waited longer.

activities.title: Describe It, Then Draw It: steps that carry a picture
activities.context: In this activity, one person describes a simple picture in words and the other draws it without seeing it. You compare the two pictures and find out how words can carry a picture, and which words are missing.

materials.item: 2 sheets of plain paper and 2 pencils
a ruler
a second person to draw

schedule.what: Describe a drawing in words, compare, and describe again with numbers and directions.

activities.record: Keep the first and second drawings and write which words made the difference.

flow.do: Your child draws a simple picture. It has a house with a door and a window. It has a tree next to the house, and a sun above. Do not let the other person see it. Sit back to back.
flow.say: Draw a house with a door, a window, a tree and a sun. Keep it hidden. In a moment, you will describe it in words, and I will draw it.
flow.kid: Draw a house, a tree and a sun. Keep it hidden.
flow.context: This is the first step of Describe It, Then Draw It. You draw a picture and keep it hidden.

flow.do: Your child describes the picture in words. The other person draws only what they hear. They may not ask questions. Compare the two drawings.
flow.say: Describe your picture in words. I will draw what I hear, but I may not ask any questions.
flow.kid: Describe the picture in words only. The other person draws it.

ask.q: How close is the drawing to the hidden one? What is different?
good: The tree is on the wrong side.
The house is the wrong size.
It is close, but not the same.

flow.context: In this step, you describe in words and compare the two drawings.

flow.do: Describe again, this time with numbers and directions. Say: the house is 6 centimetres wide, 2 centimetres from the left edge. Draw again on a fresh sheet and compare.
flow.say: Try again. This time say how big, how many and which side. For example: the house is six centimetres wide and two centimetres from the left edge.
flow.kid: Describe again. Say how big, how many and which side.

check.q: Which description lets a stranger draw the picture most exactly?
options: A house and a tree
A house 6 centimetres wide on the left, and a tree 4 centimetres tall on the right of the house
A nice house
check.why: The second description gives sizes and sides. The others leave out what the drawer needs. A wrong pick usually means the child thinks short descriptions are enough.

flow.parent: The second drawing is almost always closer than the first. The difference shows what clear steps are made of: sizes, numbers, directions and places.
flow.context: In this last step, you describe the picture again with numbers and directions.

setup.art: Two children sitting back to back at a table, one holding a hidden drawing and talking, the other drawing on a fresh sheet.
setup.caption: 1. Describe the picture in words only. The other person draws.

setup.art: Two drawings side by side on a table, one the hidden original and one the drawn copy, with a few differences circled in red.
setup.caption: 2. Compare the drawings. Say again with numbers.

projects.title: My Sprout Notebook: watch, draw and write for a stranger
projects.context: In this 7-day project, you watch moong seeds sprout in the light and in the dark, and keep a dated notebook with drawings and measurements, as Maria Sibylla Merian did with caterpillars. At the end, you write a letter so that a stranger could repeat your test.

materials.item: 2 tablespoons of whole green moong
2 small bowls or steel katoris, and 2 pieces of thin cloth
a dark cupboard or a box with a lid
a ruler marked in millimetres
a notebook, a pencil and coloured pencils

projects.safety: Moong seeds are small, so keep them away from children under five. Do not eat the sprouts raw. A grown-up should cook them first. Wash hands after touching the seeds.

schedule.what: Soak the moong, drain them, and put half in a damp cloth in the light and half in a damp cloth in the dark.
Rinse gently, look, measure the three longest sprouts in each bowl, and draw.
Rinse gently, look, measure, and draw.
Rinse gently, look, measure, and draw.
Rinse gently, look, measure, and draw.
Rinse gently, look, measure, and draw. Write down one question for next time.
Write a letter that tells a stranger how to repeat your test, and ask a friend to say which step is unclear.

projects.record: A notebook with one dated page for each day. On each page: the date, a drawing, the length of the three longest sprouts in each bowl, and one sentence on what changed. On the last page, a letter to a stranger.

flow.do: Soak 2 tablespoons of moong in water for 6 to 8 hours. Drain them. Split them between two cloths. Put one in a bowl on a window sill and one in a bowl in a dark cupboard. Wet both cloths lightly. Write the date in the notebook and draw the seeds.
flow.say: Maria Sibylla Merian watched caterpillars change for years and drew every stage. We will watch moong seeds. Will the seeds in the dark sprout? Will they look different from the ones in the light? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Soak moong seeds. Put half in the light and half in the dark. Draw them.

ask.q: Why do you think the seeds in the dark will, or will not, sprout?
good: Seeds need light to grow, so the dark ones will not.
Seeds need only water and warmth, so both will sprout.
I do not know, so we will watch.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Both bowls usually sprout. The dark sprouts are often paler and a bit longer. If neither sprouts, check that the cloth stays damp and the room is warm. Report what happens.
flow.context: This is day 1 of My Sprout Notebook. You set up two bowls and make a guess.

flow.do: Each day at about the same time, rinse each cloth gently with a little water. Measure the three longest sprouts in each bowl. Draw what you see. Write the date and one sentence on what changed.
flow.say: Rinse gently. Look closely at each bowl. Measure the three longest sprouts. Draw what you see. Write one sentence about what changed.
flow.kid: Rinse the seeds. Measure three sprouts in each bowl. Draw. Write the date.
flow.wait: Do this on days 2 to 6, about seven minutes each day.
flow.parent: Measure in millimetres, from the seed to the tip of the sprout. Measure the same three sprouts each day if you can tell them apart. Draw what you see, even on days when little changes. Dated pages are what make a notebook useful to a stranger.
flow.context: In this step, you look, measure and draw once a day.

flow.do: On day 7, your child writes a letter to a stranger on how to repeat the test. The letter says what to buy, what to do each day and what to measure. A friend reads it and underlines any step that is not clear.
flow.say: Write a letter to someone far away. Tell them how to repeat this test, step by step. Then a friend will underline anything they could not follow.
flow.kid: Write a letter to a stranger. Tell them how to repeat your test. A friend underlines the unclear parts.

check.q: Which is the best sentence for a letter that helps a stranger repeat a seed test?
options: Put some seeds in water for a while.
Soak 2 tablespoons of whole green moong in a bowl of water for 6 to 8 hours, then drain them.
Do the usual thing with moong.
check.why: The second sentence gives the amount, the kind of seed, the time and what to do next. The others leave the stranger guessing. A wrong pick usually means the child wrote as if the reader already knew.

flow.context: In this last step, you write the letter and see if a friend can follow it.

challenges.title: The Size Card: report how big something looks, so anyone can check
challenges.problem: Look at three tiny things through your water-drop lens. Make a card that tells someone far away how big each thing looks, using only everyday things for comparison, so that they can draw each one at the right size without seeing it.
constraints: Use your own water-drop lens from the experiment, or a magnifying glass.
Describe each thing by comparing it with something else, not with a number alone.
Include at least one picture of the circle with the thing drawn in it.
A second person must draw from your card without seeing the real thing.
materials: your water-drop lens, or a magnifying glass
a grain of salt, a sesame seed, a grain of rice and a single hair
a second person to test your card
general: Look at the grain of salt through your lens. Say how much of the circle it fills, for example 'half the circle'.
Compare it with a second thing: 'through the lens, a grain of salt looks as wide as a sesame seed looks without a lens'.
Draw the circle with the thing inside it. Write beside it how much of the circle the thing fills.
creative: Put the three things in order, from the smallest to the biggest, using only comparisons.
Add a scale bar on the card: a short line that stands for 'one grain of rice'.
Make the card for a younger child by using only pictures and the words 'bigger' and 'smaller'.
challenges.your_turn: Trade cards with a friend. Draw their thing from their card alone. How close is your drawing to the real thing? What word was missing?

flow.do: Tell your child that Leeuwenhoek had no ruler fine enough to measure tiny creatures. So he compared their sizes with a grain of sand and the width of a hair. Ask why he did not just give numbers.
flow.say: Leeuwenhoek compared the tiny creatures to a grain of sand and the width of a hair. Why do you think he used things like that, instead of a number?
flow.kid: Leeuwenhoek compared sizes to a grain of sand. Why not use a number?

ask.q: Why would a comparison work better than a number for a tiny thing?
good: Everyone knows what a grain of sand is.
There was no ruler small enough.
A comparison needs no tool.

flow.parent: Leeuwenhoek really did compare the sizes of tiny creatures with a grain of coarse sand and with the width of a hair, and he said how many fitted across. Today we use units like the millimetre and the micrometre, but a good comparison still helps.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Size Card challenge. You see why comparisons work.

flow.do: Look at each of the three things through your lens. For each one, draw the circle with the thing in it. Say how much of the circle the thing fills. Write a comparison. Put all three on one card.
flow.say: Look at the grain of salt through the lens. How much of the circle does it fill? Draw it. Write a comparison with something your reader knows.
flow.kid: Look at three tiny things. Draw each in a circle. Write a comparison.
flow.parent: Use the same lens, the same distance and the same coins every time. Keep a note of the hole size you used so a reader can repeat it.
flow.context: In this step, you look at the three things and make your card.

flow.do: Give the card to a second person who has not seen the things. They draw each thing from the card alone. Compare their drawings with the real things through the lens.
flow.say: Please draw each thing from this card. Do not look at the real thing. Then we will compare.
flow.kid: A stranger draws from your card. Compare it with the real thing.

check.q: A card says a grain of salt fills half the circle and is as wide as a sesame seed looks without a lens. What makes this card useful to a stranger?
options: It compares the size with things the reader knows, and gives a fraction
It uses long words
It has a beautiful drawing
check.why: A comparison with familiar things and a fraction of the circle let the reader draw it without seeing it. A wrong pick usually means the child valued how the card looked and not what it told the reader.

flow.context: In this last step, a stranger draws from your card and you compare.

setup.art: A girl looking at a grain of salt through a foil lens on coins, with a drawing of a circle half filled by a small square beside her.
setup.caption: 1. Look at a tiny thing through your lens. Draw the circle and the thing.

setup.art: Two children comparing a hand-drawn card with a drawing made from the card alone, the real salt grain between them.
setup.caption: 2. A stranger draws from the card. Compare the drawing with the real thing.

items.p: To do a test again by following the same steps is to ____ it.
items.why: A result that others can repeat from the steps becomes shared knowledge.

items.p: A girl sees something new through her lens, but nobody else can see it. What does she need before others will believe it?
opts: Clear steps that others can follow to see the same thing
items.why: A discovery is finished when other people can see it too. Clear steps let them do that.

items.p: True or false: a discovery is finished the moment one person sees something new.
items.why: False. The person may have made a mistake or been fooled. A discovery is finished when others can repeat it.

items.p: Match each word to its meaning.
pairs: The bending of light when it moves from air into water
A curved, clear piece that bends light
Asking for a claim to be checked before believing it
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: These four words explain how a water drop works and how a discovery is checked.

items.p: Sort each step: is it clear enough for a stranger to follow, or not?
items: Press the tip of a sharp pencil once into the foil on a folded towel, and twist.
Touch a toothpick tip, wet with one drop of water, to the hole.
Put your eye one finger-width above the foil.
items.a: see items
items.why: A clear step names the tool, the amount and the place. A vague step leaves the stranger to guess.

items.p: Why does a smaller, rounder drop of water usually magnify more than a bigger, flatter one?
opts: It is more curved, so it bends light more
items.why: A more curved surface bends light more strongly. That makes small things look bigger.

items.p: Explain in your own words why a drop of water can make print look bigger.
items.a: A strong answer says that light bends when it passes between air and water, and the round drop bends the light so that the print looks bigger.
items.why: A strong answer connects the bending of light to a curved drop.

items.p: The Royal Society's motto means 'take nobody's word for it'. What does that ask a scientist to do?
opts: Ask to see the evidence and check it
items.why: The motto asks scientists to check claims for themselves. It does not ask them to refuse to believe. It asks them to believe because of the evidence.

items.p: The old idea that living things can appear on their own from non-living things, such as mud, is called spontaneous ____.
items.why: Redi's jars tested this idea for flies and showed it was wrong.

items.p: True or false: if maggots appear in a jar of banana with a tight lid, the banana must have made them.
items.why: False. If maggots appear only in jars that flies can reach, the maggots came from flies. A jar with a tight lid shows no maggots if no fly got in.

items.p: Put the road of a discovery in order.
items: Others repeat the test and agree
Others doubt it and ask to check
The finding is accepted as knowledge
a: Others doubt it and ask to check
Others repeat the test and agree
The finding is accepted as knowledge
items.why: A discovery begins when someone notices something. It is shared through clear steps, meets doubt, and is settled when others repeat it.

items.p: Write one clear step, for a stranger, for the job: make a small hole in a strip of foil.
items.a: A strong answer names the tool, what to rest the foil on, how hard to press and what to do next, for example: put the foil on a folded towel, press the tip of a sharp pencil once, and twist.
items.why: A strong step names the tool, the amount and the place.

items.p: Draw a side view of a drop of water in a hole in foil. Draw two lines of light going through the drop towards an eye.
items.a: A drop with a curved top and bottom in the hole, and two lines of light that bend as they enter the drop and spread out towards an eye above.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the light bending at the curved surfaces.
items.art: A blank side view with a horizontal foil strip, an empty round hole in it, and a small eye drawn above.

items.p: Label the four parts of the water-drop lens setup: the foil, the drop, the coin stacks and the picture.
items.a: The strip across the top is the foil. The round shape in its hole is the drop. The two small piles under the ends are the coin stacks. The flat sheet at the bottom is the picture.
items.why: Each part has a job. The coins hold the foil at a fixed height above the picture.
items.art: A side view of a foil strip resting on two coin stacks above a flat picture, with a drop in the strip's hole and four empty label boxes.

items.p: Two friends in Kochi talk about a new claim.

views.says: I saw it with my own eyes. I do not need steps. I know it is true.
If nobody else can repeat it, I cannot be sure. I would like to try it myself.

items.ask: Which friend do you agree with more? Give a reason. Then say one thing the other friend has right.
items.a: A strong answer sees that others need a way to check, and that steps are what carry a discovery. It is also fair to Nila: her seeing is real and a good reason to share the steps.
items.why: Marks go for using the idea of repeating and for being fair to the other friend.

items.p: Two people follow the same steps and see slightly different pictures that agree on the main thing. What does this suggest?
opts: The main finding holds, and the differences come from hands, drops and eyes
items.why: Small differences are normal. What matters is whether the main finding appears for both people.

items.p: Why did most geologists reject Alfred Wegener's idea of drifting continents in 1912?
opts: He could not name a force strong enough to move continents, and he was not a geologist
items.why: An idea without a mechanism, from an outsider, was easy to doubt. The evidence was strong but the 'how' was missing.

items.p: Name two pieces of evidence that Wegener had for moving continents, and one thing that he lacked.
items.a: A strong answer names two of: the coasts fit, the same fossils on both coasts, matching rock layers. It names a missing mechanism, a force or process that could move continents.
items.why: A strong answer separates evidence from the missing explanation.

items.p: True or false: scientists today can measure that India is still moving, a few centimetres each year.
items.why: True. Satellites measure the movement of the plates directly.

items.p: A doubter asks, 'Can I try it myself?' Is this kind or rude?
opts: Rude, because it says you are lying
Kind, because it asks to see the evidence and does not insult
items.why: Asking to try is how science works. It treats the claim as worth checking.

items.p: Wegener's idea that the continents slowly move is called continental ____.
items.why: Today it is part of the wider idea of plate tectonics.

items.p: Sort each reason: does it explain why a good idea was rejected, or why a wrong idea was kept?
items: There was no known mechanism for how it could work.
Nobody had ever done the simple test.
It came from an outsider to the field.
It went against what most experts believed.
items.a: see items
items.why: Good ideas can be rejected because nobody knows how they could work, because they come from an outsider, or because they go against what experts believe. Wrong ideas can stay because nobody tested them, respected voices repeated them, or the story was nice.

items.p: In a famous test of flies, one jar of meat was covered with thin cloth that let smells through but not flies. What did that jar show that a sealed jar could not?
items.a: A strong answer says that the smell reached the flies outside, and they landed on the cloth, but without a way in they could not lay eggs on the meat. So the flies, not the smell or the meat, brought the maggots.
items.why: A strong answer separates the smell from the flies themselves.

items.p: Louis Pasteur boiled broth in a flask with a long, curved neck. The broth stayed clear, though air could enter. Why?
opts: Microbes in the air were caught in the bend and could not reach the broth
items.why: Air could move in and out, but the dust and microbes in it settled in the curved neck. This showed that microbes come from other microbes in the air, not from broth itself.

items.p: Match each person to what they did.
pairs: Looked at water through tiny lenses and wrote to London
Tested whether rotting meat makes maggots
Drew the ocean floor from depth numbers
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Each person did a different part of the long work of finding out.

items.p: Three of these help a discovery win belief. Which is the odd one out?
opts: Clear steps that others can follow
Others repeat the test and agree
A famous name says it is true without showing how
A new tool that shows the same result
items.why: A famous name without evidence does not help others check. The other three give people a way to see for themselves.

items.p: Two friends in Chennai talk about the Royal Society and Leeuwenhoek.

views.says: It was unfair to doubt Leeuwenhoek. He was telling the truth.
Doubting him was what the Society's motto asked for. He could be honest and still wrong, so they had to check.

items.ask: Which friend do you agree with more? Give a reason. Then say one thing the other friend has right.
items.a: A strong answer sees that honest people can make mistakes, so claims need checking whoever makes them. It is also fair to Dev: Leeuwenhoek was right, and a good doubter should help to check and not simply refuse.
items.why: Marks go for being fair to both views.

items.p: Draw three pieces of string side by side, one centimetre for each year, for waits of 3 years, 50 years and 190 years. Label each.
items.a: Three strings, one very short, one much longer, and one nearly two metres long, each labelled with its number of years.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the lengths in proportion, so the longest wait looks very long.
items.art: A blank page with space for three horizontal lines and three empty label boxes.

items.p: Here is a map of old Gondwana. Label India, the arrow showing where it moved, and the continent it was joined to in the south.
items.a: Label India as the piece on the right, draw an arrow pointing north-east, and label Antarctica or Africa as the neighbours it was joined to in the south.
items.why: India started next to the southern continents and moved north to meet Asia.
items.art: A simple map of the old southern supercontinent with empty label boxes by India, a long arrow, and Antarctica.

items.p: Anna Mani designed instruments for measuring sunshine, wind and ozone. Explain why a good instrument matters for a discovery.
items.a: A strong answer says that without a reliable instrument, different people get different readings and cannot compare. A good instrument gives the same reading for everyone, so results can be repeated.
items.why: A strong answer connects instruments to repeating.

items.p: Each fold of a sheet of paper doubles the number of layers. A sheet folded 7 times has 128 layers. How many layers after 8 folds?
items.why: 128 doubled is 256. Layers double with each fold, which is why the paper soon becomes too thick to fold.

items.p: True or false: written steps can carry every skill from one person to another.
items.why: False. Some skills, such as making a good water drop or kneading dough, are learned best by watching and doing.

items.p: Maria Sibylla Merian watched caterpillars change into moths and butterflies and drew each stage. Why is a dated drawing of every stage better evidence than a memory?
items.a: A strong answer says that memory forgets and changes, but a dated drawing records what was really seen at the time. Others can check the drawings against their own caterpillars.
items.why: A strong answer ties a dated record to checking by others.

items.p: A friend claims she can taste the difference between two kinds of salt. Plan a test that others could believe. Say what she tastes, what is hidden from her, and how a coin is used.
items.a: A strong plan has someone else prepare the two salts in identical cups, a coin flip decide which is first, the friend taste without knowing which is which, and many rounds so that luck alone would be unlikely to give a good score.
items.why: A strong plan uses blind tasting, a coin to choose the order, and many repeats.

items.p: Three people talk about whether the Royal Society should have believed Leeuwenhoek at once.

views.says: Yes. He was an honest man, and there was no reason to doubt him.
No. Anyone can make a mistake, honest or not. They should ask for a check.
They should ask for a check, and help him to share his steps, so the check can be done.

items.ask: Which person do you agree with most? Can more than one be right? Explain.
items.a: A strong answer sees that honesty does not remove the need for a check, and that helping the discoverer share steps is part of doubting well. All three have a point, though Jaya's view joins the other two.
items.why: Marks go for reasons and for being fair to the other views.

items.p: Why can some skills not be fully written down?
opts: Because the people who know them are secretive
Because they depend on a feel in the hands that comes from practice
items.why: Michael Polanyi argued that we know more than we can say. A feel for dough or for a good water drop is learned by doing.

items.p: Sort each job: can a stranger do it from written steps alone, or is it best learned by watching and trying?
cats: Best learned by watching and trying
items: Counting the seeds in an okra pod
Kneading dough to the right softness
Best learned by watching and trying
Making a round, steady drop of water
Best learned by watching and trying
Weighing out a spoon of sugar
Best learned by watching and trying
items.a: see items
items.why: Counting and measuring can be written down. Feel and balance are learned by doing.

items.p: True or false: a result that two labs on different continents get is stronger evidence than a result that one lab gets twice.
items.why: True. If different people in different places agree, a hidden problem in one place is unlikely to have fooled everyone.

items.p: Marie Tharp was not allowed on research ships but still found a valley in the sea floor. What does this suggest about who does the work behind a discovery?
items.a: A strong answer says that many people contribute to a discovery, including those who draw, compute and keep records, and they may be left out of the story. Noticing a pattern needs someone to look at all the data together.
items.why: A strong answer says that the story often leaves out important people.

items.p: In 1989 a claim of making energy in a jar of water at room temperature was dropped. Why?
opts: Other labs followed the steps and could not get the result
items.why: A claim stands when others can repeat it. When labs around the world followed the steps and found nothing, the claim was set aside.

items.p: Draw two panels. In the first, write a vague step for a job. In the second, write a clear step for the same job.
items.a: Any job, such as 'Add water' against 'Pour one cup, 250 millilitres, of water into the steel pot'.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the clear step naming the amount, the tool and the place.
items.art: Two empty comic panels side by side headed Vague and Clear.

items.p: Here is the start of a letter that tells a stranger how to repeat a seed test. Label the amount, the tool, the time and what to look for.
items.a: The amount is 2 tablespoons, the tool is a steel bowl, the time is 6 to 8 hours, and what to look for is the small white tip of a sprout.
items.why: A clear letter names all four, so the stranger does not have to guess.
items.art: A letter that says: Soak 2 tablespoons of moong in a steel bowl for 6 to 8 hours. Look for a small white tip. Four empty label boxes sit beside it.

items.p: A student says she can lift a small stone with her mind, but only when nobody is watching. What is the best reply?
opts: Ask for a test she can do while others watch, with steps that others can repeat
Ask her to do it louder
items.why: A claim that vanishes whenever it is checked cannot be tested. A fair reply asks for a test that can be repeated, and asks kindly.

items.p: Choose one thing you believe only because someone told you. How could you check it yourself, and what would you write so a stranger could repeat your check?
items.a: A strong answer names a real claim, a check that can be done at home, and a few clear steps with amounts, tools and places.
items.why: This uses the ideas on something from the child's own life.

items.p: Match each problem to its fix.
pairs: Only one person got the result
Nobody can say why it happens
Look for a mechanism and test it
The seller ran the only test
Have a separate group test it
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Each fix deals with one reason why a discovery may not be believed.

items.p: Satellites can now measure the continents moving a few centimetres each year. What does this add to the case for moving continents?
opts: A direct measurement of the movement that Wegener could not make
items.why: Wegener had fossils, rocks and coasts. A direct measurement of movement is the kind of evidence that was missing.

items.p: True or false: if two people see slightly different details through the same lens, the finding must be false.
items.why: False. Hands, drops and eyes differ. What matters is whether they agree on the main finding.

items.p: Should a new idea that is probably wrong still be tested? Who should pay for the test? Give your view and a reason.
items.a: A strong answer weighs the cost of a test against the chance that the idea is right, and notes that some surprising ideas, like drifting continents, were right. It gives a reasoned view on who pays.
items.why: There is no single right answer. Marks go for weighing cost against the chance of a surprise.

items.p: A finding that only one person has been able to get is not yet ____ knowledge.
items.why: Knowledge becomes shared when other people can follow the steps and get the same result.

quiz.p: Why did the Royal Society doubt Leeuwenhoek's report of tiny living beings in water?
opts: They did not like cloth sellers
Nobody else had a lens strong enough to check it
quiz.why: A claim that no one else can check must wait. Doubting was not rude. It asked for a way to check.

quiz.p: When is a discovery really finished?
opts: When the person writes it down
When others can repeat it by following the steps
quiz.why: A result that only one person can get could be a mistake. When others repeat it, it becomes shared knowledge.

quiz.p: Which is the clearest step for a stranger to follow?
opts: Make a small hole in the foil
Put the foil on a folded towel, press the tip of a sharp pencil once into it, and twist
Make a hole with something sharp
quiz.why: The clear step names the tool, what to rest the foil on, the number of presses and the twist.

quiz.p: A helper follows your written steps and gets a very different result. What should you do first?
opts: Tell the helper to try harder
Find the step that was unclear and rewrite it
quiz.why: If a careful person cannot follow the steps, the steps are the problem. Watching the helper shows which step to fix.

quiz.p: Why does a drop of water in a small hole make print look bigger?
opts: The curved surface bends light as it passes between air and water
quiz.why: Light bends when it passes from air into water. A round drop bends it so that small things look bigger.

quiz.p: Which drop usually magnifies more, a smaller, rounder one or a bigger, flatter one?
quiz.why: A more strongly curved surface bends light more, so it magnifies more.

quiz.p: Why did most geologists doubt the idea of moving continents in 1912?
opts: There was no evidence at all
No force that could move continents was known, and it came from outside geology
quiz.why: The evidence was strong, but the missing 'how' made the idea easy to doubt. New sea-floor evidence in the 1960s supplied it.

quiz.p: In a test with meat or fruit in three jars, maggots appeared in the open jar but not in the sealed one. What does this show?
opts: The maggots came from flies that could reach the meat
The lid made the meat fresh
quiz.why: The meat was the same in both jars. The only difference was whether flies could reach it.

quiz.p: In the Redi's Jars test with banana, flies landed and laid eggs on the cloth of the cloth-covered jar, but no maggots got into the banana. Why is this important?
opts: The smell got through the cloth, so smell alone does not make maggots
quiz.why: Smell passed through the cloth but flies could not. Without flies reaching the banana, there were no maggots. So the flies, not the smell, mattered.

quiz.p: Why can a good idea be rejected for years?
opts: Good ideas are always wrong at first
It may have no explanation yet for how it works, and it goes against what experts believe
quiz.why: An idea can be right but lack a mechanism, or need new tools to check it. Evidence can take years to arrive.

quiz.p: Which is the best reason to keep believing an old idea?
opts: Many fair tests, repeated by different people, still support it
quiz.why: Age, fame and a good story do not make an idea true. Repeated fair tests do.

quiz.p: Many discoveries rest on people who collect measurements and draw them, not only on the person whose name is on the idea. Why should those people be remembered too?
opts: Because without their data the pattern could not have been seen
Because the idea was theirs alone
quiz.why: A pattern in a pile of numbers needs someone to gather them and draw them together. Leaving these people out gives a false picture of how discoveries happen.

applications: Doctors use microscopes to find the tiny beings that cause malaria and other illnesses in a drop of blood.
Spectacles, cameras and binoculars all use lenses that bend light, as a water drop does.
Medicines are tested again by different teams before they are approved, because a result must be one that others can repeat.
Weather stations in India use standard instruments so that readings from different places can be compared.
Recipe cards, building plans and instruction sheets are methods that a stranger can follow.
Scientific journals ask authors to describe their methods so that others can repeat the work.
Citizen scientists count birds, insects and rain in many places with the same steps, so results can be added together.
Maps of the sea floor help us understand earthquakes, volcanoes and where to lay undersea cables.
Courts and engineers repeat tests under the same conditions before trusting a result.
Anyone can ask of a claim: can I try it myself, and what exactly did you do?

open_questions.q: Did the tiny beings in water exist before Leeuwenhoek saw them?
open_questions.why_open: Almost everyone says yes, but philosophers still discuss what it means for something to exist before it is known. Nobody can check by going back.

open_questions.q: How much of a skill can be written down?
open_questions.why_open: Some skills pass well in words and some only by watching and doing. Scholars still argue about how much of what we know can ever be put into steps.

open_questions.q: How many repeats are enough before we trust a result?
open_questions.why_open: More repeats make a result steadier, but there is no single number that works for every kind of test. Scientists judge each case.

open_questions.q: What are we missing today because nobody has a tool to see it?
open_questions.why_open: Every new tool has shown something that was hidden before. So there are probably things around us that we cannot see yet. Nobody knows what.

open_questions.q: How can we make sure that the people who did the work get named?
open_questions.why_open: Historians keep finding people whose work was left out of the story. There is no easy rule, and each case needs careful records.

open_questions.q: Why do some true ideas wait decades to be believed?
open_questions.why_open: Missing explanations, missing tools and the habits of groups all play a part. Historians disagree about how much each one matters in each case.

maths.problem: In a Water-Drop Lens test, hole A showed 2 dots across the circle and hole C showed 6 dots across. How many times as wide is the patch of the picture seen through C as the patch seen through A? Which lens magnifies more, and about how many times more?
maths.answer: 3 times as wide. Lens A magnifies about 3 times more than lens C.
maths.explain: 6 divided by 2 is 3. Through C you see 3 times as wide a patch. If a lens shows a narrower patch, each dot looks bigger. So A magnifies about 3 times as much as C.
maths.context: In the Water-Drop Lens test, you count the dots across the circle through three holes.
maths.why_maths: A ratio of the counts tells you how much stronger one lens is than another without needing a ruler.

maths.problem: In the Water-Drop Lens test, your counts for holes A, B and C were 2, 3 and 6. A second person, using only your steps, got 2, 4 and 6. What is the difference between the two counts for each hole, and what do the differences add up to? Do the two sets agree about the order of the holes?
maths.answer: The differences are 0, 1 and 0, which is 1 in total. Yes, both put A first, B second and C third.
maths.explain: Hole A: 2 and 2 differ by 0. Hole B: 3 and 4 differ by 1. Hole C: 6 and 6 differ by 0. The total is 1. Both people find A has the fewest dots and C the most, so they agree on the order. Small differences are normal when two people hold a drop.
maths.context: In the Water-Drop Lens test, a second person repeats your test using only your written steps.
maths.why_maths: Finding how far apart two sets of counts are shows whether the second person has really repeated your result.

maths.problem: Leeuwenhoek's claim waited about 3 years, from 1674 to 1677, before others repeated it. Wegener's idea waited about 50 years. About how many times as long did Wegener's wait last?
maths.explain: 50 divided by 3 is a little less than 17. So Wegener's wait was about 17 times as long. A claim that anyone with a good lens could check was believed fast. An idea that needed ocean maps took far longer.
maths.context: In the String of Years activity, you cut one centimetre of string for each year that a claim waited to be believed.
maths.why_maths: Dividing one wait by another turns two lengths of string into a clear comparison of how much longer the second one took.

maths.problem: Redi tested flies in 1668. The question about microbes was settled by Pasteur in 1862. At one centimetre of string for each year, how long is that string in centimetres, and in metres and centimetres? The string for Wegener's wait is 50 centimetres long. About how many Wegener strings would fit along it?
maths.answer: 194 centimetres, which is 1 metre and 94 centimetres. About 4 Wegener strings.
maths.explain: 1862 minus 1668 is 194 years, so 194 centimetres. 100 centimetres make 1 metre, so that is 1 metre and 94 centimetres. 194 divided by 50 is a bit less than 4, so about 4 strings of 50 centimetres.
maths.context: In the String of Years activity, you cut a very long string for the question of where microbes come from.
maths.why_maths: Converting years to centimetres and metres lets you hold a long wait in your hands and compare it with the others.

maths.problem: A sheet of paper is about 0.1 millimetre thick. Each fold doubles the layers. After 7 folds there are 128 layers. How thick is the stack in millimetres? After 10 folds there are 1024 layers. About how thick is that in centimetres?
maths.answer: After 7 folds, 12.8 millimetres. After 10 folds, about 10 centimetres.
maths.explain: 128 layers of 0.1 millimetre is 12.8 millimetres. 1024 layers of 0.1 millimetre is 102.4 millimetres. 10 millimetres make a centimetre, so that is a little over 10 centimetres. The stack becomes thick very fast, which is why you cannot keep folding an ordinary sheet.
maths.context: In the Doubt Round, you test the claim that paper cannot be folded in half more than about seven times.
maths.why_maths: Doubling the layers with each fold explains why a claim that sounds odd turns out to be true for ordinary sheets.

maths.problem: In a Redi's Jars test, the flies counted near the open jar on five days were 0, 2, 5, 6 and 4. Near the cloth jar they were 0, 1, 2, 2 and 1. The lid jar had none. What are the totals? How many more flies were near the open jar than the cloth jar? About how many times as many?
maths.answer: Open: 17. Cloth: 6. Lid: 0. Eleven more near the open jar, about 3 times as many.
maths.explain: 0 + 2 + 5 + 6 + 4 is 17. 0 + 1 + 2 + 2 + 1 is 6. 17 minus 6 is 11. 17 divided by 6 is a bit under 3. So about 3 times as many flies came to the open jar as to the cloth jar, and none to the lid jar.
maths.context: In Redi's Jars, you count flies near three jars of banana over five days.
maths.why_maths: Totals let you compare jars fairly across days. The pattern of the totals shows where flies could reach.

maths.problem: India moves north about 5 centimetres each year. How far is that in 1,000 years, in metres? How far in 1,000,000 years, in kilometres?
maths.answer: 50 metres in 1,000 years. 50 kilometres in a million years.
maths.explain: 5 centimetres times 1,000 is 5,000 centimetres. 100 centimetres make a metre, so that is 50 metres. 5 centimetres times 1,000,000 is 5,000,000 centimetres. 100,000 centimetres make a kilometre, so that is 50 kilometres. A movement too slow to see adds up to very far over millions of years.
maths.context: In Fit the Coasts, you learn that the continents move slowly, a few centimetres each year, and that India was once part of the old southern continent.
maths.why_maths: Multiplying a tiny yearly movement by a long time shows why nobody could see the continents moving, though Wegener was right that they do.

maths.problem: In a made-up sprout notebook, the longest sprouts in the light bowl were 3 millimetres on day 2 and 27 millimetres on day 6. In the dark bowl they were 4 and 34. How much did each bowl grow between day 2 and day 6? Which grew more, and by how much?
maths.answer: Light: 24 millimetres. Dark: 30 millimetres. The dark bowl grew 6 millimetres more.
maths.explain: 27 minus 3 is 24. 34 minus 4 is 30. 30 minus 24 is 6. The dark sprouts grew a bit more. A dated notebook makes it possible to see this, and to check it later.
maths.context: In My Sprout Notebook, you measure the longest sprouts in a bowl in the light and a bowl in the dark.
maths.why_maths: Subtracting the first measurement from the last shows how much each bowl grew, so two bowls can be compared fairly.

roots.context: In the story The Dots in the Newspaper, Anjana saw dots in a newspaper photograph. The dots became something everyone knew only when others followed her steps and saw them too. Now we ask what this tells us about how people come to know things together.

deep_truth.truth: In the Water-Drop Lens experiment, one person saw the dots first, and then others saw them by following written steps. A discovery is not finished when one person sees something. It is finished when the steps are clear enough for someone else to see it too. So knowing is something people build together, out of steps that anyone can follow.
deep_truth.habit: We often think of a discovery as one clever person suddenly seeing the answer alone. That leaves out the steps, the doubters and the people who repeated the test. They are what turn one person's sighting into something everyone knows.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Water-Drop Lens experiment, a second person counted dots using only your written steps. Where the steps were clear, your counts agreed. Where they were not clear, the counts were different until you fixed the step.

three.who_am_i: Sometimes you are the first to see something. Sometimes someone else shows you what they saw. Both matter, because a discovery needs both.
three.what_is_life: Leeuwenhoek found that a drop of pond water holds many living beings, swimming, feeding and turning. Life was there all along, in places nobody had thought to look.
three.what_is_this_world: The world is much bigger than what the eye alone can see. Each new tool, from a drop of water to a satellite, shows another part of it, and people have to learn together how to read what the tool shows.

roots.thread: A discovery starts with one person seeing something. Before others believe it, it meets doubt, and it needs clear steps, tools and the work of many people. By the end it is no longer one person's idea. It is something a whole community can check and agree on, and can change when new evidence arrives.

how_we_found_out.story: For thousands of years, many people believed that rotting meat makes maggots by itself. It seemed obvious, because maggots always appear on old meat. In 1668, an Italian doctor named Francesco Redi, living in Florence, wondered if the maggots came from tiny eggs laid by flies. He put pieces of meat in jars. He left some jars open. He sealed some, and he covered some with a thin cloth. Maggots appeared in the open jars, where flies could land. They did not appear on the meat in the sealed jars. On the cloth, flies laid eggs, but the maggots could not reach the meat. Redi wrote down the test so others could repeat it. Other people did, and the idea that flies come from meat was set aside. The same question about microbes was settled much later, in the 1860s, by Louis Pasteur.
how_we_found_out.who: Francesco Redi, an Italian doctor and naturalist in Florence
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: Many people believed that maggots were made by rotting meat itself, an idea called spontaneous generation. Redi's three kinds of jar showed that maggots appear only where flies can lay eggs on the meat.

playtest: Read as a parent and child in a city flat would use it, but not yet tried at home. The Water-Drop Lens needs kitchen foil, a pin, a pencil, a pen, a toothpick, four coins and a colour newspaper photograph. It is the least certain part: how many dots appear across the circle depends on the drop and the print, so the counts may be small, and the steps give a fallback of counting letters of the smallest print. A drop that falls through the hole is fixed by a smaller drop on a fresh toothpick. Redi's Jars needs a week, and fruit flies usually come within 2 to 5 days in warm weather, which the steps say; if no flies come, the unit says to report that honestly. A grown-up seals the jars at the end. The sprout project needs a rinse each day; the sprouts are not to be eaten raw. To verify before publishing: the Leeuwenhoek dates (letters from 1674, Hooke and others repeating in 1677, made a member in 1680), Wegener's dates, the Marie Tharp and Bruce Heezen details, the Anna Mani details, the Gallivan folding story (a very long roll, twelve folds, 2002), the ibn al-Haytham paraphrase, India's yearly movement of about 5 centimetres, and the three videos, whose YouTube addresses are still to be found.
